turn_text: It's a big issue in Ohio. We're one of the top five states in the country in terms of overdose deaths from heroin, prescription drugs. But it's even worse than that. It's not just the people who are dying as tragic as that is. It's so many people who are getting lost. I spent the last few days actually in mostly rural Ohio talking about this issue because it's not an inner city or a suburban or rural issue. It's everywhere. And frankly, in many of our rural communities, it's worse than anywhere per capita at least. And so we've got to do something. I did work on legislation these last three years to get at this problem. We brought in experts from around the country, including a lot of Ohio experts, to say, what's working? What's not working? How do we spend our federal dollars more effectively? The result of that is the Comprehensive Addiction and Recovery Act. It's called CARA. The President just signed it about two weeks ago. It's now going to start to be implemented. It'll provide more funding for treatment, which is important. But important for me, and I talked to some of the Farm Bureau folks today who are working on this. By the way, applaud the Ohio Farm Bureau for the work they're doing on this is prevention. You know, 4-H is a great way to help prevent, as is Junior Fair, and because it gets young people engaged in something positive, constructive. But frankly, we need to do a much better job at a younger age of telling young people what the dangers are inherent in getting involved with these drugs. Sometimes it's inadvertent, as you know. People go in, get a procedure, an operation. They are given prescription drugs that are addictive. They get addicted, literally physically addictive. And then getting into heroin, fentanyl, and all these other issues, very, very, very dangerous. And frankly, the best people to go into the schools and so on to talk about it are probably the people who have been through it. But the Farm Bureau gets that. I talked to two Farm Bureau families today who told me about experiences in their own families, one in FU, one in Nice, who had unfortunately become addicted. So it's a big issue. This bill will help. Better prevention, education, better treatment, longer term recovery. It also helps law enforcement support it by 250 groups around the country who care about this issue. We got to get this bill implemented and then ultimately it's going to be solved in our communities.
